claims.text: Retention of toughness in high-entropy alloys is controlled by preventing grain-boundary precipitation.
A homogeneous, single-phase nanocrystalline or ultrafine-grained solid solution has high toughness.
A homogeneous single-phase microstructure minimizes crack-nucleation sites.
Annealing above a critical temperature induces elemental segregation and precipitation at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary precipitates act as stress concentrators and embrittle the material.
Embrittlement caused by grain-boundary precipitates lowers alloy toughness.
The deposited W-Ta-Cr-V refractory HEA can have a single-phase BCC microstructure containing nanocrystalline and ultrafine grains.
The as-deposited W-Ta-Cr-V-type HEA exhibits high toughness.
Crossing from below 1023 K to above 1023 K promotes grain-boundary segregation and precipitation.
Thermomechanical exposure can induce a secondary HCP phase in a refractory HEA.
The induced HCP phase can be concentrated at grain boundaries.
Annealing produces Cr-V-rich nanometer-scale grain-boundary precipitates in the proposed W-Ta-Cr-V system.
High configurational entropy and lattice distortion suppress diffuse segregation at lower annealing temperatures.
Above a thermal threshold, elemental-migration kinetics overcome entropy stabilization and cause selective grain-boundary precipitation.
Grain-boundary precipitates reduce local grain-boundary cohesion.
High-temperature annealing will reduce toughness or ductility relative to an as-deposited or low-temperature-annealed baseline.
The magnitude of toughness loss increases with the volume fraction and connectivity of grain-boundary precipitates.
Chemical complexity and lattice distortion initially favor a stable single-phase structure in the relevant refractory HEAs.
At very high temperatures, very long annealing times, or outside the relevant composition range, mechanisms other than grain-boundary precipitation may dominate toughness.
